title: Remembering without hatred
hook: the Ardas names martyrs, not enemies; memory is for courage, not revenge

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rattan Singh Bhangu, who set the hard century down in verse. Your line was the chronicler. Whose story did you write down, or wish you had? Today, what Sikhs do with all that memory. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

Partway through the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings, there's a passage that's hard to hear. It remembers Sikhs who were cut limb from limb. Sikhs whose scalps were taken. Sikhs broken on the wheel, sawn apart, who gave their heads and kept their faith. The congregation stands with folded hands and answers Waheguru after it. And then something is missing. Listen for the names of the governors, the generals, the invaders who did these things. They aren't there. Today: remembering without hatred.
screen: `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` → `CUT, SCALPED, BROKEN, SAWN.` → `AND NOT ONE ENEMY IS NAMED.`

segments.voice: Start with what the prayer keeps. The Ardas names the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Piare, and then the ones whose names are lost, by what they endured and what they held on to. Their hair, their faith, their Guru. The focus is on the ones who stood, not on the ones who struck. That's the first thing. Memory pointed at courage. The second thing is the line Guru Arjan left in the Guru Granth Sahib, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That's a hymn from a Guru who was himself put to death, and it can be heard alongside the long list of martyrs. It doesn't say nothing bad happened. It says the heart doesn't have to be organized around the people who did it. The third thing is how the prayer ends. After all that suffering, the Ardas closes by asking for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. Everyone. Not everyone except them. The same prayer that remembers the wheel and the saw asks for the well-being of the whole world. And this connects to something the path met a few weeks back: a minister whose grief turned into a slaughter. Sikhs tell that story too. Read this way, the Ardas keeps grief from being handed on as hatred. So when Sikhs stand and remember, the prayer doesn't ask who to pay back. It asks, in effect, could I stand like that? Courage, not revenge.
screen: `THE PRAYER NAMES THOSE WHO STOOD.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY, NO ONE A STRANGER.` · `IT ENDS ASKING THE GOOD OF ALL.` · `HATRED IS NOT HANDED ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE, NOT REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to remember without anger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who went through something hard, in your family or your own life. Let yourself see it plainly. Now notice where your attention goes. If it keeps drifting to the person who caused it, gently bring it back to the one who endured. What did they hold on to? How did they stand? Stay there. If anger rises, let it pass through like weather, and come back. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings. It names the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and ends asking the good of all. Today's word.
Your line: courage, not revenge. Today, when an old hurt comes up, steer the story toward who stood up, not who knocked you down. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas at the close of services and daily prayers; one passage remembers the martyrs by what they endured, the congregation answers Waheguru, and the prayer closes asking for the good of all.

fork.setup: you're putting together the words a whole community will pray, standing, every day. you have to remember people who were tortured to death. what do you put in?
options: the names of the men who did it, so nobody forgets.
what the martyrs endured and kept, and a closing wish for everyone's good.
nothing at all, it's too painful.
fork.reveal: the Ardas does the second: it remembers the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and closes with sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

what a scholar hears: the martyrs' passage is built around deeds and steadfastness, and it sits between the remembrance of the Gurus and the closing sarbat da bhala, so courage, not grievance, is what the prayer hands on.

notes: The martyrs' passage of the Ardas is paraphrased (cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, sawn apart, gave their heads but kept their faith); confirm the list and that no persecutor is named anywhere in the standard Ardas.

Ang 1299 (Kanra, Guru Arjan, 'na ko bairi nahi bigana, sagal sang ham kau ban aai') paraphrased as 'no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone'; confirm Ang and paraphrase.
'the close of Sikh gatherings' describes the Ardas's use; confirm the wording is fair.
The link back to day 857 (the minister whose grief turned on the Sikhs) is a callback, not a new claim.
No dates or numbers in the voice.
Editor pass: hook no longer opens 'Listen' (day 875 did) and the garbled 'standing prayer said standing' is fixed; the persecutor line is reframed so the prayer, not the narrator, carries the point.

Audit: martyrs' passage placed 'partway through' the Ardas (it sits mid-prayer, before the Takhts and petitions, not near the end); narrator claims that Sikhs read Ang 1299 alongside the martyrs and that the Ardas 'is built' to stop hatred softened to readings.
